topics.label: Git Fundamentals
topics.desc: The distributed version control system tracking content as a graph of commits, where each clone holds full history; the foundational tool for nearly all modern software work.

topics.label: Staging & Commits
topics.desc: The git add staging area lets you assemble a precise snapshot before git commit records it with a message, separating what changed from what you choose to capture.

topics.label: Branches
topics.desc: Lightweight movable pointers to commits, created with git branch, checkout, and switch, that let work proceed in isolation so features develop without disturbing the main line.

topics.label: Merging
topics.desc: Combining branch histories with git merge, producing either a fast-forward or a three-way merge commit that joins divergent work into a single integrated branch.

topics.label: Rebasing
topics.desc: Replaying commits onto a new base with git rebase to keep history linear; interactive rebase (-i) also squashes, reorders, and edits commits before sharing them.

topics.label: Resolving Conflicts
topics.desc: Manually reconciling overlapping changes Git can't auto-merge, editing conflict markers then staging the result, often aided by an editor or mergetool three-way view.

topics.label: Reset vs Revert
topics.desc: git reset moves the branch pointer to rewrite local history (soft, mixed, hard), while git revert safely records a new inverse commit to undo already-published changes.

topics.label: Stashing
topics.desc: git stash shelves uncommitted changes onto a stack so you can switch context with a clean working tree, then restore them later with stash pop or apply.

topics.label: Cherry-Pick
topics.desc: git cherry-pick copies the changes from a specific commit onto the current branch, useful for backporting a fix or pulling one commit out of another branch.

topics.label: Tags
topics.desc: Named references marking specific commits, typically annotated tags like v2.1.0 used to label releases and trigger CI/CD publish pipelines on push.

topics.label: .gitignore
topics.desc: A pattern file telling Git which untracked paths to ignore, keeping build artifacts, node_modules, secrets, and editor files out of the repository.

topics.label: Reading Log & Diff
topics.desc: Inspecting history and changes with git log, git diff, git show, and git blame to understand what changed, when, why, and who authored each line.

topics.label: Git Hosting Platforms
topics.desc: Hosted services like GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket that store remote repositories and layer pull requests, issues, CI, and project management around plain Git.

topics.label: Remotes & Sync
topics.desc: Named pointers to hosted repos (origin, upstream) synchronized with git fetch, pull, and push, the mechanism that shares commits between your clone and the team.

topics.label: Pull / Merge Requests
topics.desc: The proposal to merge a branch, opened as a GitHub pull request or GitLab merge request, bundling diff, discussion, review, and CI checks before integration.

topics.label: Code Review Etiquette
topics.desc: The practice of reviewing peers' diffs constructively with specific, kind, actionable comments on small focused PRs, to catch bugs and share knowledge without ego.

topics.label: Forking & Upstream
topics.desc: Cloning a repo under your own account to contribute via PRs, then keeping it current by adding an upstream remote and syncing the original project's changes.

topics.label: Branching Strategies
topics.desc: Team conventions for how branches flow, from heavyweight Git Flow to lightweight GitHub Flow and trunk-based development with short-lived branches and feature flags.

topics.label: Conventional Commits
topics.desc: A commit-message convention (feat:, fix:, chore:) that encodes intent so tools can auto-generate changelogs and derive semantic version bumps via semantic-release.

topics.label: Semantic Versioning
topics.desc: The major.minor.patch scheme signaling breaking changes, features, and fixes, letting consumers and release tags communicate compatibility expectations across versions.

topics.label: Protected Branches
topics.desc: Rules guarding main that require passing CI checks, approving reviews, and up-to-date branches before merge, enforcing quality and preventing direct pushes.

topics.label: Agile Values
topics.desc: The Agile Manifesto's mindset favoring individuals, working software, customer collaboration, and responding to change over rigid plans, the philosophy underlying Scrum and Kanban.

topics.label: Scrum Framework
topics.desc: An iterative framework organizing work into fixed-length sprints with defined roles, events, and artifacts, the most widely adopted way teams operationalize Agile delivery.

topics.label: Sprint Events
topics.desc: Scrum's recurring ceremonies: sprint planning, the daily standup, the sprint review or demo, and the retrospective where the team inspects and adapts its process.

topics.label: Scrum Roles
topics.desc: The three accountabilities in Scrum: the product owner owning priorities and backlog, the scrum master facilitating process, and the developers delivering the increment.

topics.label: Kanban & WIP Limits
topics.desc: A pull-based flow method visualizing work on a board across columns and capping work-in-progress per stage to expose bottlenecks and improve throughput.

topics.label: User Stories
topics.desc: Short feature descriptions from a user's perspective (As a..., I want..., so that...) with acceptance criteria, the unit of work teams plan and deliver each sprint.

topics.label: Estimation
topics.desc: Sizing work relatively with story points and techniques like planning poker, trading precise time guesses for shared understanding and predictable sprint capacity.

topics.label: Backlog Refinement
topics.desc: Ongoing grooming of the product backlog, clarifying, splitting, and re-prioritizing upcoming items so they're ready and estimated before a sprint pulls them in.

topics.label: Issue Trackers
topics.desc: Tools like Jira, Linear, and GitHub Issues that capture stories, bugs, and tasks as tickets, organizing the boards, sprints, and workflows the whole team works from.

topics.label: README
topics.desc: The front-door document of a repository explaining what a project is, how to install and run it, and how to contribute, the first thing any new reader opens.

topics.label: Technical Writing
topics.desc: The skill of writing clear, concise, well-structured docs for a target audience, using examples, headings, and plain language so readers find answers fast.

topics.label: API Documentation
topics.desc: Reference material describing endpoints, parameters, and responses, often generated from OpenAPI/Swagger, JSDoc, or TypeDoc so consumers can integrate without reading source.

topics.label: Architecture Decision Records
topics.desc: Lightweight Markdown files capturing a significant technical decision, its context, options, and consequences, giving future maintainers the why behind the architecture.

topics.label: Comments vs Docs
topics.desc: Knowing when to explain why in code comments versus capturing how and what in external docs, favoring self-documenting code and comments that age well over time.

topics.label: Diagrams & UML
topics.desc: Visual models of systems and flows using Mermaid, draw.io, Excalidraw, or UML notation to communicate architecture, sequences, and data relationships at a glance.

topics.label: Docs-as-Code
topics.desc: Treating documentation like source: written in Markdown, versioned in Git, reviewed in PRs, and built with tools like Docusaurus, MkDocs, or Astro Starlight.

topics.label: Changelogs
topics.desc: A human-readable record of notable changes per release following Keep a Changelog conventions, often auto-generated from conventional commits at version time.

topics.label: Written & Async Communication
topics.desc: Conveying ideas clearly in writing across Slack, email, and tickets so distributed teammates can act without a meeting, the dominant mode of modern collaboration.

topics.label: Remote Collaboration
topics.desc: Working effectively across distance and time zones using video calls, shared docs, and overlap norms, compensating for lost hallway context with deliberate structure.

topics.label: Giving & Receiving Feedback
topics.desc: Exchanging specific, timely, behavior-focused feedback and receiving it without defensiveness, the engine of growth in code reviews, one-on-ones, and retrospectives.

topics.label: Pair & Mob Programming
topics.desc: Collaborative coding where two (pairing) or more (mobbing) developers work at one screen, sharing context and catching issues live, often via VS Code Live Share.

topics.label: Asking Good Questions
topics.desc: Posing well-researched, reproducible questions with context and what you've already tried, respecting others' time and following norms like 'don't ask to ask'.

topics.label: Stakeholder Communication
topics.desc: Translating technical work and trade-offs into outcomes that non-engineers (product, design, leadership) understand, aligning expectations and surfacing risk early.

topics.label: Blameless Culture
topics.desc: A team norm treating failures as systemic learning opportunities rather than individual fault, embodied in blameless postmortems that make people safe to be honest.

topics.label: Continuous Learning
topics.desc: The habit of steadily learning amid fast-moving tech through docs, courses, side projects, and reading code, the core survival skill of a long software career.

topics.label: T-Shaped Skills
topics.desc: Pairing broad familiarity across many areas with deep expertise in one, the balance between the generalist-versus-specialist poles that makes developers versatile yet valuable.

topics.label: Building a Portfolio
topics.desc: Demonstrating ability through public work, a GitHub profile, shipped projects, a personal site, or writing, evidence that speaks louder than a resume to employers.

topics.label: Open-Source Contribution
topics.desc: Participating in public projects by filing issues, sending PRs, and reviewing, building skills, reputation, and network while giving back to tools you depend on.

topics.label: Networking
topics.desc: Building professional relationships through communities, conferences, meetups, and platforms like LinkedIn, a leading source of opportunities, mentors, and collaborators.

topics.label: Mentorship
topics.desc: Accelerating growth by learning from senior peers and later guiding juniors, a two-way exchange that compounds skill, judgment, and confidence on both sides.

topics.label: Imposter Syndrome
topics.desc: The common feeling of being a fraud despite real competence; recognizing it as near-universal and reframing self-doubt helps developers keep learning and contributing.

topics.label: Time Management
topics.desc: Prioritizing and protecting focus with techniques like timeboxing, deep-work blocks, and saying no, defending the uninterrupted attention that real engineering requires.

topics.label: AI Coding Assistants
topics.desc: LLM-powered tools like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, and ChatGPT that autocomplete, generate, and refactor code, now a standard part of the developer workflow.

topics.label: Agentic Coding Tools
topics.desc: Autonomous coding agents like Claude Code that plan and execute multi-step tasks, reading files, running commands, and editing across a repo rather than just suggesting lines.

topics.label: Prompt Engineering for Code
topics.desc: Crafting clear instructions, context, and constraints so an AI produces correct, idiomatic code, the leverage skill that determines how useful coding assistants actually are.

topics.label: AI Review & Explanation
topics.desc: Using AI to explain unfamiliar code, summarize diffs, and surface bugs or smells, a fast first-pass reviewer and onboarding aid for legacy or third-party code.

topics.label: Verifying AI Output
topics.desc: Critically reviewing, testing, and running AI-generated code rather than trusting it blindly, guarding against hallucinated APIs, subtle bugs, and confidently wrong answers.

topics.label: AI Tests & Docs
topics.desc: Delegating boilerplate to AI by generating unit tests, docstrings, READMEs, and commit messages, then reviewing the output to amplify productivity on tedious work.

topics.label: Limitations & Responsible Use
topics.desc: Understanding AI's pitfalls, hallucinations, outdated knowledge, security and licensing risks, and data privacy, and using assistants responsibly without leaking secrets or skipping review.
